newsitem.title: USA: Toyota 4-Runner blamed in $7.6 million jury award.
newsitem.headline: Toyota 4-Runner blamed in $7.6 million jury award.

text.p: A jury has awarded $7.6 million to a woman paralyzed from the neck down when the 1994 Toyota 4-Runner in which she was riding rolled over in an accident.

The Multnomah County Circuit Court jury in Portland deliberated three days after a three-week trial before blaming faulty design of the sport-utility vehicle for the May 1994 accident that left Linda McCathern, 38, a quadriplegic.
"The vehicle should not have rolled over," McCathern's attorney Jeffrey Foote said. "It was too tall and too narrow."

While many sport-utility vehicles have come under fire for their tendency to roll over in accidents, the verdict against Toyota Motor Corp., its sales division and a local dealer was believed to be the first against the popular 4-Runner, which has been on the market since 1984.
Foote said Toyota lengthened the vehicle and reduced its height in the 1996 model year, improving its safety. "They took steps they should have taken 10 years ago," he said.
McCathern's cousin, Elizabeth Sanders, was driving the vehicle at night on smooth, dry pavement in eastern Washington when she swerved to avoid an oncoming vehicle.

The car rolled over twice before coming to rest on its wheels, still on the road, Foote said. Sanders and two young children in the back seat were not badly hurt but McCathern suffered a crushed vertebra that left her unable to make any movements beyond shrugging her shoulders or moving her head.
The driver of the oncoming vehicle was never located.

Attorneys for Toyota argued that the accident occurred when a tire blew and said any car would have rolled in similar circumstances. They offered no comment after the verdict and could not be reached Friday.
Foote, who originally asked for $18.5 million, said the proceeds of the award would be used to pay for the 24-hour a daycare required by McCathern, who has a 5-year-old daughter.

McCathern had been in the news before the accident because her husband allegedly abducted their twin daughters and took them to his native Libya. At the time of the accident she had just won permission from the Libyan government to visit the girls, who are now 14, Foote said.
